scenes.heading: Circles: circumference and area
scenes.say: Pizzas, wheels and running tracks are all circles. You can't count squares to measure them. Instead you need a special number called pi. Let's find out how it works.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Roll a wheel one full turn: the track is just over 3 wheel-widths long
scenes.science: Circumference ÷ diameter = π ≈ 3.14 for every circle
scenes.breaks: A real tyre squashes a little, so measuring isn't perfect, but π is the same for every perfect circle.
scenes.say: Paint a dot on a bike wheel and roll it one full turn. The track it leaves is just over three times as long as the wheel is wide. That number, a little over three, is pi. It's about three point one four, for every circle.
scenes.caption: Roll a wheel one full turn. The track is just over 3 times the wheel's width. That number is π, about 3.14, for every circle.

scenes.heading: Parts of a circle
scenes.say: The radius goes from the centre to the edge. The diameter goes right across, so it's twice the radius. The circumference is the distance around. And pi is about three point one four one five nine. Use the pi button on your calculator.
scenes.caption: Radius: centre to edge. Diameter: right across, twice the radius. Circumference: distance around. π ≈ 3.14159.

scenes.heading: Parts of a circle
scenes.say: First the circle and its centre. The radius goes from the centre to the edge. The diameter goes right across through the centre, so it's two radii. The circumference is the distance around the edge.

scenes.heading: The two formulas
scenes.say: Circumference is pi times the diameter, or two pi r. Area is pi r squared. Only the radius is squared, so if you're given the diameter, halve it first. A handy rhyme: cherry pie is delicious, apple pies are too.
scenes.caption: C = πd = 2πr. A = πr². Halve the diameter first. Rhyme: cherry pie is delicious (C = πd), apple pies are too (A = πr²).

scenes.heading: Area example
scenes.question: Find the area of a circle with diameter 12 m, to 1 decimal place.
scenes.say: Find the area of a circle with diameter twelve metres. First halve it: the radius is six. Six squared is thirty-six. Pi times thirty-six is about one hundred and thirteen point one square metres.
scenes.caption: Diameter 12 m, so r = 6 m. 6² = 36. A = π × 36 ≈ 113.1 m².

scenes.heading: Semicircle: curve plus diameter
scenes.say: Here's a semicircle with diameter eight centimetres. Its perimeter has two parts: the curved edge, which is half the circumference, and the straight edge along the bottom.
scenes.caption: A semicircle with diameter 8 cm. Its perimeter is the curved edge (half the circumference) plus the straight edge.

scenes.heading: Semicircle perimeter
scenes.question: Find the perimeter of a semicircle with diameter 8 cm, to 1 decimal place.
scenes.say: Now a semicircle with diameter eight centimetres. The curved part is half of pi times eight, about twelve point five seven. Don't forget the straight edge, eight centimetres. Add them: about twenty point six centimetres.
scenes.caption: Curved part: ½ × π × 8 ≈ 12.57 cm. Straight edge: 8 cm. Total ≈ 20.6 cm.

scenes.heading: Don't mix them up
scenes.say: Circumference is a length around the edge, measured in centimetres or metres. Area is the space inside, measured in square units, and it's the formula with the square in it.

Quick recap. The diameter is twice the radius. Circumference is pi d. Area is pi r squared. For a semicircle, take half and add the straight edge for perimeter. And round only at the end. Now try the practice questions!
scenes.caption: d = 2r. C = πd = 2πr. A = πr². For a semicircle, take half and add the straight edge. Round only at the end. Now try the practice questions!
